payload.rationale: The event requires NASA GISS’s reported unsmoothed annual Land–Ocean Temperature Index for 2026 to be strictly above both 1.28°C and the 2025 value. Equality does not qualify; another dataset’s hottest-year designation would not suffice. My 25% estimate is a background-climate judgment, not a forecast informed by observed 2026 temperatures. Long-term warming and the exceptional warmth of recent years make crossing this threshold plausible. However, annual variability—particularly ENSO and associated ocean-temperature changes—can offset the warming trend, and 2025 could impose a hurdle higher than 1.28°C. The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is that cooler ocean conditions or an unfavorable already-observed 2026 trajectory may have made the threshold difficult to reach. The strongest reason it could be too low is that persistent exceptional ocean warmth or a warming ENSO transition may already have put 2026 on a record-setting trajectory. Without current observations, I cannot distinguish these possibilities reliably.
limitations: No outside evidence records were supplied, and no browsing or tools are available.
The supplied information contains neither the 2025 NASA GISS annual value nor 2026 monthly temperatures or ENSO observations.
By the September cutoff, much of the year has elapsed; those unavailable observations could materially change this estimate.
Resolution depends on NASA GISS’s reported annual index and applicable reporting precision and revisions, not on other temperature datasets.
